chapter: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
title: Bassist Harry Gray becomes president of the Chicago union local
summary: Horace and the band campaigned for bassist Harry Gray, who handled the payroll, to run for president of the Chicago musicians' local; Jesse Simpkins replaced him.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, during that time we would play dance music, and it would give the people a chance to dance, and sometimes we'd have some nice dancers, even, just from our guests that were there, you know. ^ Had some fun. They'd do all this swing, and a lot of them would do the twist and all that stuff. I think I would like to inject one thing while we're talking about that band. This is an important fellah. My bass player, in that band, was named Harry Gray, G-R-A-Y, whom we campaigned, and almost had to fight to run for the presidency of the musicians' local in Chicago. This was Harry Gray, and he played

bass, and he was always a figurehead. He was a good man. I used to have him pay the fellows off, you know, and keep books and all this sort of stuff, and he was a good figurehead. He was pretty accurate, and he was a well-to-do man, and we campaigned for him, and he won the presidency in Chicago, and he did an awful lot there. Naturally, I had to get another bass player, and the bass player that followed him was a guy named Jesse Simpkins. He was an excellent bassist, and he was from my home town. He was a little kid, I remember, when I was coming up, and he could play.
